chapter: Ensemble, harmony and the Ory band
title: Silence, holes and ensemble integration of the front line
summary: DeVore explains leaving holes in the lead so clarinet and trombone can fill in, contrasting New Orleans with Dixieland, Kid Thomas and Doc Evans, and the discipline this requires.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Is that important? What? What about silence then? Is that important? Oh, yeah.

Particularly for a cornet player. You see, when a cornet player is playing a lead, he should play it not abruptly, melodically and smoothly, leaving what I call holes for the other one to fill in. Like, I'm on this You Tell Me Your Dream Jimbo, that's the last tune Jim played last time. You play la, da, la, da, da, and there's a pause there, see. And then the clarinet, do, do, do, do, do, that eighth note thing. And you go la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, But now some trumpet players like Doc Evans for instance, that's all he talks about. Well guys never play straight enough, but Doc will play. He'll play. See, it's going all the time and there's no room.
Well what about the clarinet play? Should he be going all the time?
Yeah, yeah. He'd be driving on. He doesn't have to do it.
He doesn't have to phrase it.

See, here's the way for ensemble, which is the most important thing and it's the hardest to get the integration of the front line. To integrate, you have the clarinet play going here and basically this is what amounts to. He plays a straight lead and when the holes come, the clarinet fills in and the trombone fills in. And you can have a lamellia line here with a fill in line starting here and back and forth. A Dixieland style is very cut and dried, like a Phil Napoleon band. When the clarinet player stops, the clarinet player starts. When the clarinet player stops, the clarinet player starts. It's all like this. But New Orleans style, you have a clarinet player here and maybe he'll start here, start here, start here, anywhere. The clarinet might start at any point.

But of course, and it's taken for granted, he'll be playing when the clarinet player drops out. Like the Thomas band, Thomas plays the straightest lead of anybody in town. More so than a person, anybody. Short, hot notes. With the biggest gaping holes. And then the guys are always filling in like Manuel Paul or Louis Nelson. But a clarinet player, the silence angle is extremely important because he's got to drop out so there's room for the other men. So you have the band sound rather than just a bunch of individuals playing. That's why an all-star band sounds bad. Not in all instances, you know. But when I'm thinking of the popular conception of an all-star band, a bunch of guys are whiz-bangs on their instruments. Everybody playing all at once. I've heard Doc Evans' band play when it's knock your ear drums down. Because everybody just go in the town all at once and there's no holes. So where you've got things switching back and forth between trombone, clarinet, and trumpet.
But this goes back to the conception of discipline and form.

Discipline and form, yeah. Well that's it. That's why New Orleans music is such a disciplined music. Because you've got to force yourself. Particularly if you've got the technique to do anything you want to do. Then you've got to discipline yourself and force yourself to do these things. To play the style. You wouldn't have to do that but then you're not playing real New Orleans styles.
